title: Moin Moin
localName: Moin moin — moimoi, steamed bean pudding
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Peeled beans blended very fine and frothy, then beaten a further eight minutes and five more after the oil — the air is what makes it set rather than go dense.
longDesc: Moin moin is a steamed bean pudding and the whole thing turns on aeration. The beans are soaked only ten minutes, pulsed so each one splits and the skin falls off, finished by hand, then blended very fine with stock and peppers until frothy. After that comes the work: eight minutes of mixing to beat air in, then five minutes more once the oil and seasonings are folded through. Wrapped in banana leaves and steamed forty to fifty minutes, it sets into something smooth and light. Under-beaten, it comes out as a brick.
ingredients: Banana leaves, or any containers for steaming
2 cooking spoons vegetable or sunflower oil
Smoked or raw prawns, or corned beef (optional)
// Used in the method but not listed in the original
equipment: Stand mixer, hand mixer or a wooden spoon
Foam sponge, for washing the leaves
steps: Soak the beans 10 minutes, then pulse a few times in a jug blender so each bean splits and the skin falls off. Finish peeling by hand.
Blend the peeled beans with the stock, peppers and onion until smooth — very fine and frothy, with no lumps.
Mix the batter approximately 8 minutes with a stand or hand mixer, or a wooden spoon, to incorporate air.
Melt the palm oil if using, let it cool, and add it to the batter with the vegetable oil.
Add the bouillon cubes, crayfish and salt. Adjust the consistency with stock or water until it is semi-fluid but definitely not watery, and mix 5 additional minutes.
Shred the mackerel and fold it in with the other proteins.
Wash the leaves with a foam sponge and salt, and remove the stalks.
Fold the leaves in doubles, put 2 spoonfuls of batter in each, add a boiled egg whole or halved, and fold over.
Arrange in a steamer, or line the pot with the leaf stalks and leaves. Keep the water beneath the moin moin, not submerging it.
Cover tightly and steam 40 to 50 minutes on medium heat until set, topping up the water as needed.
chefTips: Thirteen minutes of beating, total, in two stages. This is not optional and it is what separates moin moin from a dense bean block.
Fold, do not beat, once the peppers and seasonings are in — over-mixing at that stage knocks the air back out.
Semi-fluid but definitely not watery. Too loose and it will not set; too thick and it steams unevenly.
Ten minutes is all the soak the beans need. Longer and they absorb water and go bland.
Pulse to peel, do not blend. You want each bean to split so the hull sloughs off.
Water beneath, never over. Submerged moin moin becomes bean soup.
Banana or uma leaves cook fastest, then foil, then plastic or aluminium plates — which take longest. Factor that into your timing.
commonMistakes: Over-mixing after the peppers go in.
Letting the water cover the parcels.
Batter too thin, so it never sets.
sources: Adapted from 'Moimoi – Steamed Bean Pudding', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantities as printed: 3 Cups Brown/Black Eyed Beans, 2 cooking Spoon vegetable/Sunflower oil, 1 Cup Chicken Stock (Optional), 2 Bell pepper (Tatashe) or Shombo, 1 Onion, 1 Atarodo, 3 Tablespoons Ground Crayfish, 1 Small Boiled or Smoked Mackerel (Titus), Smoked or Raw Prawns/Corned Beef (Optional), 4 Boiled Eggs, 2 Bouillon Cubes, Salt to taste. The 8-minute mix, the 5 additional minutes, the 2 spoonfuls per portion and the 40-to-50-minute steam are all hers.

Her peeling instruction, verbatim: 'soak the beans for 10 minutes then, using the pulse function on your jug blender, pulse a few times. This will cause each bean to split and the skin to fall off. Then pour in a bowl and complete peeling by hand.'

LIST/METHOD MISMATCH, flagged: the method says 'Melt palm oil (if using), cool, then add to batter along with vegetable oil' — palm oil is NOT in the ingredient list and no quantity is given anywhere. It is listed above under a clear heading rather than silently inserted.

NOTE: 'Smoked or Raw Prawns/Corned Beef (Optional)' carries no quantity. Yield is not explicitly stated; '2 spoonfuls batter per portion' from 3 cups of beans implies a count the author does not give.

DISAGREEMENT on bean soak time before peeling, including within this author's own work: 10 minutes for moin moin, 5 minutes in lukewarm water for her akara (NGA028), 3 to 5 minutes (Ajoke, NGA005), overnight refrigerated (1Q Food Platter, NGA023). She gives no reason for her own difference.

DISAGREEMENT on technique: the peppers are blended raw into the batter here; 1Q Food Platter pre-cooks a stew and folds it in (NGA023). And 1Q gives NO aeration step at all, where this recipe gives 8 minutes plus 5. Steam times agree closely, 40 to 50 against 40 to 45.

The wrapping-versus-time note in the tips is from All Nigerian Recipes (NGA024): 'The Moi Moi that gets done quickest is the one wrapped in Uma or Banana leaves, followed by Moi Moi wrapped in aluminum foils then the one that takes the most time is Moi Moi cooked in aluminium or plastic plates.'
storage: 4 days refrigerated, 2 months frozen in its wrapping.
reheating: Steam 10 minutes, or microwave in the leaf.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas are high in plant protein, folate and soluble fibre.
Egg and fish add complete protein and omega-3 fats.
culturalNote: Moin moin is one of the most portable foods in Nigeria — wrapped, steamed, eaten cold or hot, sold by hawkers and served beside jollof at every party. The leaf matters more than it looks: uma leaf and banana leaf both perfume the pudding in a way foil cannot, and moin moin elepo, the palm-oil version, is remembered by writers as the hawker's cry that reached the brain before the food did.
